title: Coulomb's law and the electric field: forces between charges, worked through
examples: What is the force between two 1 microcoulomb charges 10 cm apart?
Why does electric force fall with distance squared?

explain.say: Rub a balloon on your hair and it lifts the strands without touching them. In 1785 Charles-Augustin de Coulomb measured that invisible push with a delicate torsion balance. On the board is his law in action: the force between two charges of 1 microcoulomb each, plotted against their distance apart.

draw.text: Coulomb's law and the electric field: forces between charges, worked through

explain.say: Coulomb's law: the force equals k times the two charges multiplied, divided by the distance squared, where k is about 9 billion in SI units. For two 1 microcoulomb charges 10 centimetres apart, that works out to 0.9 newtons, about the weight of a small apple. Like charges repel, unlike charges attract. What happens if you double the distance?

The force drops to a quarter, 0.225 newtons at 20 centimetres. That's the inverse-square law, the same shape as gravity, and you can see the curve plunge as the charges move apart. Halve the distance to 5 centimetres and the force jumps to 3.6 newtons. How many times bigger is that than at 10 centimetres?

draw.text: Double r  ⇒  F falls to a quarter

explain.say: Four times. Now the electric field, E, the force per coulomb that a tiny test charge would feel. At 10 centimetres from a 1 microcoulomb charge, E is k Q over r squared, 900 thousand newtons per coulomb. With several charges, you add the fields as arrows. Here two charges push a test charge, and their up and down parts cancel, leaving a net push to the right. Why did they cancel?

Because the two charges sit symmetrically, one above and one below. Adding arrows like this is called superposition. Wonderful work! Real-world link: laser printers and photocopiers put toner exactly where an electric field pulls it. Challenge: two 2 microcoulomb charges sit 10 centimetres apart. What is the force between them?

draw.text: Superposition: the total field is the vector sum of every charge's field.

faq.a: The force between two point charges is k times the product of the charges divided by the square of their distance, with k about 9 times 10 to the 9. Like charges repel and unlike charges attract.
A quantity that falls with the square of distance: double the distance and it drops to a quarter. Electric force, gravity and the light from a point source all follow it.
asks: Why does force fall with distance squared?

faq.a: The electric field at a point is the force a small positive test charge would feel there, per coulomb of its charge. It is measured in newtons per coulomb, or volts per metre.
With several charges, the total force or field is the vector sum of the contributions from each charge on its own.
asks: How do you add electric fields?

faq.q: What is the constant k in Coulomb's law?
faq.a: k equals 1 over 4 pi epsilon nought, about 8.99 times 10 to the 9 newton square metres per coulomb squared. Epsilon nought is the permittivity of free space.

facts: Charles-Augustin de Coulomb published his law of electric force in 1785.
The constant k in Coulomb's law is about 8.99 billion newton square metres per coulomb squared.

quiz.say: Two charges 3 metres apart feel a force of 4 newtons. What is the force when they are 6 metres apart?
quiz.show: Two charges 3 m apart feel a force of 4 N. What is the force when they are 6 m apart?
quiz.why: Doubling the distance divides the force by 2 squared, which is 4, so 4 newtons becomes 1 newton.

wrong.1: Halving would be a one over r law; Coulomb's law is one over r squared.
wrong.2: Moving apart weakens the force, it never strengthens it.

quiz.say: Two negative charges are placed near each other. What do they do?
quiz.show: Two negative charges are placed near each other. They...
quiz.why: Like charges, both negative here, repel.

wrong.1: Attraction happens only between opposite charges.
wrong.2: Any two charges exert a force on each other.
